o1.biggest_strength: It plans all 24 posts with hooks, within capacity, and leads with sleep and narrator clips in the evening. The week 1 drafts use our customers' own words ('brain still on', 'replaying emails', 'quit by day three') in our warm voice.
o1.biggest_mistake: It says no post needs review but does not plan a submission for borderline later posts like 'Awake at 2am'. It also tacks on a live-stream idea, which risks scope creep and pushes the length past 1,200 words.
o1.what_would_make_it_a_10: Flag which week 2 to 4 hooks could trigger review and batch-submit them on 16 November. Drop the bolt-on live idea to stay within length.

o2.biggest_strength: It handles review timing cleanly by batch-submitting weeks 2 to 4 on 16 November. The success measures are sensible and include a caveat that the 5.9% narrator save rate comes from a small sample of 5 posts.
o2.biggest_mistake: Weeks 2 to 4 get only one-line weekly angles, not post-level hooks, so the plan is less usable past week 1. Batch-submitting 18 posts on day one also puts unspoken pressure on the team.
o2.what_would_make_it_a_10: Add a 24-post hook grid like a real calendar, and say who writes the weeks 2 to 4 posts and when so the 16 November batch is realistic.

reason: Both make the right calls on sleep, narrators, evenings and the stop list. Output 1 gives me a full 24-post calendar and sharper customer hooks, so I could run it tomorrow, though Output 2 thought the review process through more carefully.
